title: Tracking Learner Progress Across Grade 6 to Grade 9
h1: Tracking Learner Progress Across Grade 6 to Grade 9
description: How Kenyan schools track CBC learner progress from KPSEA in Grade 6 through junior school to KJSEA in Grade 9 — without reducing it to one number.
author: SQUL Team
quickAnswer: Tracking progress from Grade 6 to Grade 9 means following the same learner across KPSEA, a Grade 7 baseline, Grade 8 growth and KJSEA — by learning area, strand coverage, attendance and support needs. It is a trajectory, not a single number, and it should inform teaching and transition rather than predict a final result.
intro: **Quick answer:** a learner's CBC story runs from Grade 6 to Grade 9 across two national assessment points and three years of school-based evidence. To track it, keep the same learner identity, capture a baseline at the start of Grade 7, record strand coverage and levels each term, and read the trajectory by learning area. This guide explains how to track learner progress from Grade 6 to Grade 9 across KPSEA, junior school and KJSEA. It is part of the [complete guide to CBC assessment management](/blog/cbc-assessment-management-complete-guide).

The transition from primary to junior school is where records most often break. The learner moves to a new class, often a new school, and the receiving teachers see a KPSEA result but not the strand history behind it. By Grade 9, the school is making senior school placement decisions with a thin view of how the learner got there.
This guide explains what to track, how to establish a baseline, how to avoid turning progress into a prediction, and how to use the record in parent conversations and transition planning.

sections.heading: Why the story gets lost between Grade 6 and Grade 9

blocks.text: CBC assessment is cumulative, but school records are often organised by year and by class. A learner can move from Grade 6 to Grade 7 with a KPSEA result, a report card and a file of certificates — and no strand-level history that the new teacher can use.

items: **New school, new record.** The receiving school starts a fresh file and never sees the primary evidence.
**New teachers, new standard.** Grade 7 teachers interpret the rubrics independently of the primary school.
**KPSEA becomes the whole story.** A single national result is treated as a complete description of the learner.
**Terms are recorded, not trajectories.** Each report card is filed separately, so nobody sees the direction of travel.
**Support plans restart.** A learner who needed help in Grade 6 is identified again in Grade 8, after two lost years.

blocks.text: The exact national report formats and timelines are set by KNEC. The school's job is to keep the **local record** that sits underneath them: the strands, the evidence, the support and the attendance.

blocks.title: Do not average performance levels
blocks.text: EE, ME, AE and BE are descriptors, not points on a continuous scale. Converting them to numbers and averaging them creates a false precision — and a number that cannot be explained to a parent.

sections.heading: The Grade 7 baseline is the missing link

blocks.text: A baseline is not a repeat of KPSEA and not a mini-KJSEA. It is a short diagnostic in the first few weeks of Grade 7 that tells the teacher what the learner can do now, in this school's curriculum and language.

items: **Keep it short.** One task per learning area is enough to establish a starting point.
**Use the same sub-strand language** as the term's curriculum map, so the baseline connects to teaching.
**Do not grade it for the report card.** It is a placement and planning tool, not a summative event.
**Record it in the same learner record** as the rest of the term, tagged as a baseline.
**Share the pattern with the class teacher**, not a ranking of learners.

blocks.title: A baseline is a map, not a label
blocks.text: The purpose is to know where to start teaching, not to decide who is “good” at a subject. The moment it becomes a label, it stops being useful.

It is tempting to use Grade 7 and Grade 8 data to predict a Grade 9 result. Resist it. A prediction based on a handful of levels is fragile, and it can become a self-fulfilling expectation for the learner.

items: **Use the trajectory to plan support**, not to set a target level.
**Look for direction and consistency**, not a precise forecast.
**Ask what changed** when a learner moves up or down — a new task, a new teacher, an attendance issue.
**Keep the learner in the conversation.** A trajectory is a description, not a destiny.

blocks.text: The earlier the signal, the cheaper the response. A conversation in Grade 7 is worth more than a crisis meeting in Grade 9.
Parents understand progress better than they understand levels. Show the direction, name one strength, name one next step, and explain what the school is doing.

In Mathematics, your child moved from approaching to meeting expectations between Grade 7 and Grade 8, and the Grade 8 evidence shows they can now handle ratio problems. The next step is explaining their reasoning in writing.
blocks.cite: A progress conversation, not a prediction

items: **Avoid comparing with another learner.** Compare with the learner's own earlier evidence.
**Explain the level in plain language.** “Meeting expectations” is not “average”.
**Name the evidence.** A parent trusts a level more when they can see the task behind it.
**Be honest about gaps.** A missing strand is a plan, not a secret.

sections.heading: Using the record for Grade 9 transition

blocks.text: By Grade 9, the learner is not only producing a result; they are choosing a senior school pathway. The progress record should inform that conversation alongside interests, aptitudes and the learner's own view.

items: **Look across learning areas**, not only at the strongest subject.
**Consider strand-level strengths** — a learner may be stronger in a particular strand than the overall level suggests.
**Include attendance and support history**, because they explain the trajectory.
**Listen to the learner.** The record is evidence, not a decision.
**Share the record with the receiving school** where appropriate and with consent.
The same learner identity (UPI and assessment number) is used across grades.
KPSEA results and support notes are attached to the learner record.
A Grade 7 baseline exists in every learning area.
Levels and strand coverage are captured each term.
Attendance is part of the progress view.
Support plans have an owner and a review date.
The school can show movement over time, not just the latest level.
Parent conversations use the learner's own trajectory.
Grade 9 transition conversations use more than one data point.
The record can be transferred with the learner.

blocks.text: SQUL keeps the learner's assessment history across grades and terms, so a teacher can see where a learner started, what has changed and which strands still need work.

items: **One learner record** from primary through junior school.
**Baseline and term assessments** in the same history.
**Strand coverage and level movement** rather than a single average.
**Attendance and support notes** alongside achievement.
**Transferable records** for learners who change school or campus.

faqs.question: Can I compare KPSEA and KJSEA results directly?
faqs.answer: They are different assessments at different stages, with different contributing components. You can describe a learner's trajectory across them, but a direct numerical comparison is misleading. Compare learning-area patterns and the evidence in between.

faqs.question: What is a good measure of progress under CBC?
faqs.answer: A combination of level movement over time, strand coverage, assessment completion and attendance. Avoid averaging performance levels; they are descriptors, not points on a scale.

faqs.question: What about learners who join in Grade 7 or Grade 8?
faqs.answer: Run the same baseline, attach whatever prior record the learner brings, and mark the missing history explicitly. Do not invent prior levels; use the baseline as the starting point.

faqs.question: How do we share progress with parents?
faqs.answer: Use the learner's own trajectory, one strength and one next step, with the evidence behind it. Avoid comparing with other learners or predicting a final result.

faqs.question: Does the Grade 9 record determine senior school placement?
faqs.answer: KJSEA and the learner's performance inform placement, alongside interests and other criteria. The school's progress record is valuable for guidance and support, but it does not replace the official placement process.
